editorial:
Imagine stepping back into the gritty, loud world of New York City in the late 70s. You get to hang out with two wild punk musicians who are being grilled by a rock journalist. It feels more like a fly-on-the-wall documentary than a scripted movie. Since it was a student project, the whole thing has a raw, messy energy that fits the punk rock scene perfectly. You can tell the director was just soaking up the chaos of the time, especially with the real footage from the legendary CBGB club. It is less about a big plot and more about the funny, awkward chemistry between the musicians and the guy trying to make sense of their noise.

What really works here is how natural the dialogue feels. It does not feel like actors reading lines; it feels like a real conversation. The pacing is quick, though it can feel a bit choppy since it was an early student film. If you love music history or just want to see where the punk movement started, you will really dig this. Since it is a rare find, you should look for it on a high-quality archive or add the physical Blu-ray to your collection to keep the 16mm look. It is a great piece of history for any movie buff.
endingExplained: The film wraps up by showing the clash between the polished world of journalism and the messy world of punk. After the interview, you see that the musicians aren't interested in fame or following rules. They stay true to their rebellious roots while the journalist is left trying to figure them out. It ends on a light note, proving that the spirit of punk is about being yourself, no matter how strange you seem to others.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves punk rock history and indie films.
